html:
A Greek hand-cranked device of bronze gears that modelled the movements of the sun and moon and predicted eclipses. It was made probably in the 2nd century BCE and is often called the oldest known analogue computer.

Sponge divers found it in 1901 in an ancient shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Greek mainland. It came up as lumps of corroded bronze. Only X-ray work, and above all CT scans from 2005, showed what was inside: some thirty surviving gears and thousands of tiny inscribed letters.

Turning a handle moved pointers on its dials. It showed the sun and moon in the zodiac, the phase of the moon, and the dates of eclipses decades ahead. One dial tracked the four-year cycle of games such as the Olympic Games.

No other geared device this fine survives from the ancient world, and nothing of its kind appears again until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe. It builds on Greek astronomy such as that of Hipparchus. Cicero wrote of a similar sphere made by Archimedes and taken to Rome, which suggests such machines were rare but not unique.
sum: A Greek hand-cranked device of bronze gears that modelled the movements of the sun and moon and predicted eclipses. It was made probably in the 2nd century BCE and is often called the oldest known analogue computer.
